idiom_name: struct of function pointers + state pointer (hand-built vtable)
implementation_notes: C has neither classes nor interfaces, so the object adapter is built by hand with two structs: the target is a struct of function pointers, the adapter is a struct holding a state pointer to the adaptee plus the callbacks that translate calls. Every callback casts its state pointer back and delegates, so the translation site is explicit and the struct must be initialised before the first call. C99 designated initialisers make that wiring readable and keep the vtable and its context in one place; a small wrapper layer over an existing C API (turning descriptors into a typed reader, say) is the same pattern at function granularity. Choose the vtable form when several implementations must share one target header - it is a conventional C encoding of dynamic dispatch - and prefer plain wrapper functions when only a signature changes.
pitfalls: The void *ctx handle erases type information: a callback registered with the wrong context type compiles and corrupts memory at run time.
The adapter struct must outlive every call that receives it; returning a pointer to a stack-allocated adapter leaves dangling state.
C has no constructors, so forgetting to initialise a function-pointer member leaves a null pointer that only traps at the call site.
Copying the adapter struct copies the state pointer, not the adaptee - two adapters then share one mutable adaptee with no ownership rule.

variants.name: Thin adapter functions over a void * context
variants.implementation_notes: When only the call signature differs, skip the vtable: write a wrapper function with the signature the caller expects, translate the arguments and delegate, passing extra state through the extra void *userdata argument that C callbacks conventionally carry. This is how callback-based APIs are adapted without inventing an object, and the same trick simulates a closure (context plus function pointer). Choose it for one-operation adaptations and for callback compatibility; reach for the vtable form when the caller needs a value with several interchangeable operations.
pitfalls: The convention is not enforced: a callback invoked without its userdata, or with the wrong one, is silent undefined behaviour.
The context struct must stay alive for the whole iteration; a callback stored beyond the call must copy the context onto the heap and free it later.
Adapting a function pointer to a different signature discards the argument types - keep the translation in one function and comment the ABI it expects.
